html:
The Innu, also called the Montagnais, are a First Nations people of eastern Quebec and Labrador in Canada. They call their homeland Nitassinan, "our land". The word Innu means "people".

For thousands of years their ancestors lived as hunters and gatherers in the northern forest. They followed caribou, moose and small game inland in winter, travelling by snowshoe and toboggan, and came down to the coast and the rivers in summer to fish and hunt seals. They lived in portable tents of skins or bark.

The Innu language belongs to the Cree, Montagnais and Naskapi dialect continuum, close to Cree and unrelated to the Inuit languages of their northern neighbours. The Innu are broadly divided into the Montagnais of the forested south and the Naskapi of the north, who differ in dialect and partly in way of life.

Europeans met them early. Basque whalers worked the Strait of Belle Isle in the 1500s. In 1603, at Tadoussac, Innu leaders made an alliance with Samuel de Champlain. That alliance, aimed against the Haudenosaunee, shaped the founding of New France, and Innu hunters were early partners in the French fur trade. Across the strait, on Newfoundland, lived the Beothuk.

Missions, epidemics and, in the 1900s, dams, mines and military low flying over Labrador changed their land. Today about 29,000 Innu live in communities and reserves in Quebec and Labrador.
sum: The Innu, also called the Montagnais, are a First Nations people of eastern Quebec and Labrador in Canada. They call their homeland Nitassinan, "our land". The word Innu means "people".
